title: Room for more than one position
statement: An argument task's prompt and sources must leave room for more than one defensible position.
detail: An AP evaluator lists arguability as a hard-fail dimension for long essays and document-based questions, and an outside judge's rubric fails a document set when all documents point to one obvious conclusion. An exploit study found the check passes when the rubric notes merely list two opposing thesis sentences, and recommended that the judge verify both are genuinely defensible from the curriculum. One way is to weigh one cause against another rather than confirm a single primary cause. A check must confirm that each alternative is really defensible, not merely opposed, that each source bears on the prompt and that the scoring guide is fully earnable from what the course teaches.
against: in one evaluator's report, document-based items passed overall at 99.1% while only 27.3% passed its document-diversity check, so a related rule did not gate the result. Official prompts also use 'primarily' when they pose two alternatives, so the judge's dislike of 'primary cause' framing may be its own preference. The gain after banning that framing, +15.9 points, came on 20 essay items, and the project counted swings of ±14 points at 17 to 24 items as not statistically meaningful; specification failures were still 88% of the remaining essay failures (`icloud-work/ap-social-studies-generator/data/model_findings.md`).
